A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and contain readable main text, equations, Figures 1–2, and Appendices A–H. The substantial reformatting does not prevent reliable comparison.

before.justification: Section 7 reports original Monte Carlo simulations of the product-selection game, using 30,000 trials per setting. Figure 1 presents results varying human rationality and assistant private information.

after.justification: Section 7 and Figure 1 retain the original product-selection simulations and their results, including the reported 30,000 trials per setting.

M1.justification: The POAG model, observation-interference definitions, Boltzmann selection policy, and optimal k-interference procedure remain unchanged. The expanded explanation of modeling RLHF within POAGs introduces no new implemented algorithm.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same synthetic product-selection game under rationality and private-information variations. Newly mentioned commercial assistants and the locked-door illustration are contextual examples, not additional evaluations.

E2.justification: Figure 1 compares the same k-interference policies, including zero interference. No evaluated comparator is added or removed; the expanded RLHF discussion does not introduce an experimental baseline.

E3.justification: Both versions retain five products, independently uniform attributes, expected reward as the outcome, the same rationality sweep, and the same private-observation and interference ranges. No experimental setting or testing procedure is revised.

E4.justification: The rationality and private-information sensitivity experiments are retained. Although v2 shortens Section 6, Figure 2 and Appendix E preserve the supplementary analysis of how Boltzmann rationality affects interference incentives.

E5.justification: Both versions report 30,000 Monte Carlo trials per setting. Neither adds seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, significance tests, or another uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: v2 omits Section 6's explicit numerical threshold, β ≈ 0.77361, above which interference is preferred in Example 6.2. The corresponding curve remains in Figure 2, and the simulation curves and other reported numerical results are unchanged.

T1.justification: The existing formal definitions, numbered results, and appendix proofs are retained. The new Computational Complexity passage adds a limited theoretical argument that sharing all private information converts the DecPOMDP setting into a POMDP, invoking PSPACE-completeness to motivate communication.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain the three incentives for interference and the distinction between action-level necessity and policy-level avoidability. The abstract and relocated concluding discussion retain the claim that interference can benefit humans even under perfect value alignment.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive qualifications about communication costs and comprehension, computational obstacles to optimal policies, and the need to test other human models and human subjects. It also explains interference through physical actions and suggests transparency and override controls.

D1.justification: v2 removes the statement that experiments ran on a Google Colab CPU runtime. Appendix H retains the same software-library disclosures. This is a loss of implementation information, not evidence of changed hardware or rerun experiments.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to The Off-Switch Game, textbooks by Koller–Friedman and Russell–Norvig, and four sources concerning contemporary assistants. It elaborates the relationship to RLHF and clarifies its distinction from earlier information-in-games research without replacing the central positioning.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized explanatory rewrites, expands the CUDA example, rearranges parts of Section 5, and trims Section 6. It reorganizes concluding material into limitations, an Impact Statement, and Computational Complexity discussion, while retaining the main section and appendix sequence.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the single-column main text with an ICML two-column layout, changes the title and affiliation presentation, and introduces running headers. Appendices use wider text, and both figures are enlarged and repositioned while retaining their plots and captions.

improvement.justification: v2 improves interpretability through clearer interference examples and more explicit communication, computational, and human-model limitations. These modest gains outweigh the loss of the numerical threshold and hardware disclosure. The underlying simulations and principal proofs remain unchanged.
